title: Your mind goes blank in an interview
lede: They ask a question you have absolutely prepared for. Nothing arrives. There is a silence you can hear, and inside it a loud voice explaining that you are losing this.

blocks.text: They ask a question you have absolutely prepared for. Nothing arrives. There is a silence you can hear, and inside it a loud voice explaining that you are losing this.

items: Blanking is a physiological event, not evidence about your ability. Under adrenaline, blood moves away from the retrieval functions you need. Fighting it with effort makes it worse; the exit is a state change, not harder searching.
Interviewers are not scoring fluency. Most are quietly scoring whether you are steady under pressure — which means a visible, calm recovery scores higher than a smooth answer.
Silence feels roughly four times longer to the person inside it. What feels like a collapse reads to them as someone thinking.

items.move: Say out loud that you are taking a moment
items.detail: Naming it converts a freeze into a deliberate pause. It also stops the spiral, because you are no longer hiding anything.

items.move: Do one slow exhale and put your feet flat
items.detail: A long out-breath is the fastest lever you have on your own nervous system. It buys you a few IQ points immediately.

items.move: Restate the question in your own words
items.detail: This is not stalling. Restating reliably retrieves the material, because you are giving your brain a cue instead of a demand.

items.move: Start with a concrete example, not a thesis
items.detail: Specifics are stored more accessibly than abstractions. Begin with a time, a place, a problem, and the answer assembles itself as you speak.

items.move: If it is still gone, park it honestly and return
items.detail: Ask to come back to it. Almost every interviewer says yes, and almost none holds it against you.

items.say: "Give me a second on that one — I want to give you a real example rather than a general answer."
"So you're asking about a time I had to change direction after committing publicly. Yes — last spring..."
"I have gone blank on that, which is annoying because I have a good answer. Can we come back to it in a few minutes?"
"Can I go back to your earlier question? Here is what I was reaching for."

items: Filling the silence with words while you search. Rambling is remembered; a three-second pause is not.
Apologising repeatedly. One acknowledgement is composure; three is a story about your nerves.
Inventing a fake example under pressure. Follow-up questions dismantle it.
Explaining that you are nervous, in detail. It moves their attention from your answer to your state.
Writing off the interview internally. The recovery is often the thing that gets noted.
Send a short follow-up with the answer you wanted to give. It is legitimate, it is rare, and it demonstrates exactly the composure they were testing.
Practise your five core stories out loud, standing up, not in your head. Silent rehearsal does not build retrieval under adrenaline.
Treat the blank as data about your preparation format, not about your worth.

limit: This is a bad twenty minutes, not an emergency — the only real risk is what you do afterwards. Do not invent experience you do not have to recover the moment; a fabricated answer that gets you hired becomes a dismissal risk later. If panic attacks are happening repeatedly in high-stakes moments, that is worth a conversation with a doctor.
